Affiliate programs sit in a strange middle ground for most SaaS founders: too passive to take seriously, too potentially lucrative to ignore. The reality is that the top SaaS affiliate programs generate 10-30% of total revenue through a network of motivated promoters who do the marketing work without a salary. ConvertKit has over 10,000 affiliates. Notion's community affiliate program became a growth flywheel. Most SaaS affiliate programs, however, generate close to nothing. The difference isn't traffic volume or brand recognition — it's structure. This guide covers what that structure looks like, from commission model to affiliate type to the churn trap that kills programs quietly.

Commission Structure: The Decision That Sets Everything Else

Your commission structure is the most important decision you'll make when launching an affiliate program. It determines who signs up, how hard they promote you, and how sustainable the program is long-term. Three models dominate SaaS affiliate programs: Recurring commissions (20-30% of monthly subscription) are the gold standard for motivated affiliates. When a promoter earns every month a customer they referred keeps paying, they have a financial incentive to send you quality leads and stay engaged with your program long-term. ConvertKit's 30% recurring commission is the benchmark. At 20-30%, a single enterprise referral can generate hundreds of dollars per month indefinitely. This model attracts serious content creators and niche influencers who think long-term. One-time commissions (50-100% of the first month's payment) generate faster affiliate payouts and work well for lower-priced products where recurring commissions would be too small to motivate. The problem is that affiliates have zero incentive to care about the quality of the customers they refer — churn is your problem, not theirs. This model also creates a payout spike that doesn't match the revenue you actually retain. Hybrid models (lower recurring percentage plus a one-time first-payment bonus) balance immediate motivation with long-term engagement. They're more complex to communicate but often perform better than either pure model. The right choice depends on your average contract value, your churn rate, and who your target affiliates are. For B2B SaaS above $50/month, recurring commissions almost always win.

Affiliate Platform Selection: Don't Build It Yourself

Running an affiliate program on spreadsheets and manual PayPal transfers is a conversion killer. Affiliates expect proper tracking, a dashboard showing their performance, and reliable payouts. The platforms that handle this vary widely in price and capability. PartnerStack at around $500/month is the enterprise option — deep integrations, multi-tier programs, and a marketplace where affiliates can discover your program. If you're doing serious volume, it's worth the price. It also hosts a directory of active B2B affiliates looking for new programs, which accelerates recruitment. FirstPromoter and Rewardful both sit around $49/month and are the right starting point for most SaaS companies. They integrate cleanly with Stripe, handle recurring commission calculations automatically, and provide affiliates with a clean dashboard. Rewardful has a slight edge on Stripe integration; FirstPromoter is more flexible with commission rules. Impact and ShareASale are affiliate networks rather than pure program management tools. They bring built-in affiliate audiences but take a percentage of commissions and add complexity. Most SaaS founders should start with a dedicated platform before going to a network. For payouts, Stripe Connect is the simplest solution for global affiliates — it supports multiple currencies and integrates with most program platforms. PayPal works for smaller affiliates who prefer it but creates friction for international payouts due to fees and currency conversion.

Affiliate Types: Who Actually Drives Revenue

Not all affiliates are equal. Understanding the four types and which to prioritize will save you months of effort recruiting the wrong people. Content affiliates — bloggers, YouTubers, newsletter writers in your niche — are the highest quality affiliate type for B2B SaaS. They produce evergreen content that ranks in search ("Best LinkedIn automation tools" or "ConvertKit vs Mailchimp") and sends you qualified traffic for years. They're harder to recruit because they're selective about what they promote, but their audience trust translates directly to your conversion rates. Influencer affiliates have large social followings and can generate traffic spikes. The quality of the leads varies widely depending on how closely their audience matches your ICP. A LinkedIn influencer promoting a LinkedIn tool to their engaged B2B audience can be exceptional. A general tech influencer mentioning your tool in a YouTube video is often noise. Tool review sites (G2, Capterra, Trustpilot, and niche comparison sites) are passive but powerful. Someone searching "best project management software" on a comparison site is in active buying mode. Getting listed and collecting reviews on these platforms is table-stakes, and many offer paid affiliate partnerships on top of organic listings. Resellers and agency partners are underutilized by most SaaS companies. A digital marketing agency that recommends your tool to every client and handles the setup for them isn't just an affiliate — they're a distribution channel. These relationships require more investment to establish but produce referrals with very low churn because the agency is accountable for the client's success.

Cookie Duration: The B2B Detail Most Programs Get Wrong

B2B SaaS purchase decisions take time. A founder who discovers your tool through an affiliate's blog post might take three weeks to evaluate alternatives, get budget approval, and convert. If your cookie expires in 7 days, the affiliate gets no credit — and no motivation to keep promoting you. A 30-day cookie is the absolute minimum for B2B SaaS. The companies with the strongest affiliate relationships offer 90-day cookies. This aligns with the reality of B2B sales cycles and reduces the friction of affiliates worrying about losing credit for referrals they clearly influenced. Set your cookie duration at 90 days and make it a selling point in your affiliate recruitment pitch. Most of your competitors default to 30. Differentiate on this.

Recruitment Strategy: Quality Over Quantity

A program with 10 active, motivated affiliates who understand your product outperforms a program with 500 passive sign-ups who never promoted a single user. Recruitment quality matters more than recruitment volume. The highest-ROI recruitment strategy is direct outreach to complementary SaaS tools with different ICPs. A company selling email marketing software to the same audience as your LinkedIn tool isn't a competitor — they're a potential affiliate partner who already has your exact customer's trust. Reach out, propose a reciprocal arrangement, co-create content, and formalize it with your affiliate program. For content affiliates, search for existing content about your category. If someone has already written a "best tools for LinkedIn automation" post, they're a natural affiliate candidate. They've already demonstrated interest in your niche. Reach out with a personalized pitch, offer them an extended trial, and give them the data they need to write a genuine review. Affiliate directories on PartnerStack and Impact also surface affiliates actively looking for new SaaS programs to promote. These are warm prospects who understand the affiliate model and need minimal education.

The Churn Trap: Why Affiliate Customers Churn More

This is the variable most affiliate program guides skip. Customers acquired through affiliates churn 20-30% faster than customers acquired through other channels. The reason is qualification. When a content affiliate writes a broad review post targeting everyone in a niche, some percentage of the referrals won't be a good fit for your product. They sign up because of the affiliate's recommendation, not because they have a specific problem your product solves. They try it, don't find the immediate value they expected, and cancel. Mitigation strategies: add a qualification step in your affiliate onboarding (a short use case survey that gates the affiliate link) so referred users have to self-select their fit. Build a specific landing page for affiliate traffic that speaks directly to the affiliate's audience. And monitor affiliate-specific churn by tracking the cohort of customers from each affiliate source. If a particular affiliate's referrals churn at 2x your average rate, that affiliate is a cost center, not a revenue driver — even if their gross referral volume looks strong.

Success Metrics: What to Actually Track

The three affiliate program metrics that matter: Affiliate-generated MRR — the monthly recurring revenue from customers referred by affiliates, tracked by cohort. This is the number that justifies the program's existence. Affiliate conversion rate — the percentage of visitors an affiliate sends who start a trial, and the percentage of those who convert to paid. This tells you which affiliates are sending qualified traffic versus volume. Cost per acquisition via affiliate — total affiliate commissions paid divided by new MRR generated. Compare this to your CAC from paid channels. If your affiliate CPA is lower than your paid CPA, scale the affiliate program. If it's higher, audit affiliate quality.

Building an Affiliate Program That Lasts

The affiliate programs that become serious revenue drivers share common traits: generous recurring commissions that attract long-term thinkers, reliable tracking and payouts that build trust, active affiliate support (a Slack channel, monthly performance updates, new content to promote), and a focus on quality referrals over raw volume. Start small. Launch with 10-20 carefully selected affiliates before opening the program publicly. Refine your materials, commission structure, and onboarding based on their feedback. Then scale with the playbook you've validated. The goal isn't a passive income channel. It's a distribution network built on other people's trust — and that takes deliberate construction.
